title: From Darjeeling to 2,000 Walmarts: Indian Tea Gets Its Zero-Tariff American Moment
excerpt: A new US-India trade deal eliminates duties on Indian tea, giving exporters a competitive edge over China just as brands like Vahdam are scaling up coast to coast.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian tea exports to the US can rise to 20 million kilograms due to zero tariffs.
  • Vahdam Teas has secured shelf space in 2,000 Walmart stores across the US.
  • The US tea market, valued at $13 billion, is shifting towards premium offerings.
  • Indian brands are leveraging authenticity and direct sourcing to compete globally.
  • The Indian American community is embracing authentic tea options in mainstream retail.

The Hindu BusinessLine
For decades, Indian tea in America meant one of two things: a generic box of Darjeeling at the grocery store, or a milky, cardamom-laced cup at your neighbourhood Indian restaurant. Neither did justice to a country that is the world's second-largest tea producer, harvesting over 1.3 billion kilograms annually across estates stretching from Assam to the Nilgiris. That is changing fast, and the shift has as much to do with trade policy as it does with taste. ## The Zero-Duty Breakthrough Under the interim US-India trade agreement framework finalised earlier this year, Indian teas are set to receive zero-duty access to the American market — a dramatic reversal from 2025, when exporters faced stiff 50 percent tariffs that caused order cancellations and forced discounts across the supply chain. "India exported 15.2 million kilograms of teas to the US last year," Anshuman Kanoria, chairman of the Indian Tea Exporters Association, told The Hindu BusinessLine. "Now, we can go back to 18 to 20 million kilograms because of the zero-duty on Indian tea exports." The tariff elimination hands India a critical competitive advantage over China, its main rival in the US tea market. Chinese tea exports to America still face tariffs under the broader trade framework, creating a pricing edge that Indian exporters intend to exploit. "Over China now we have a duty advantage," Kanoria said. "The ease of doing business and scope of growth is much more now in the US market." ## Vahdam's Walmart Play If the trade deal opens the door, Indian brands are already walking through it. The most visible example is Vahdam Teas, the direct-to-consumer brand founded in 2015 by Delhi entrepreneur Bala Sarda when he was just 23 years old. The company now sells to 104 countries and has secured shelf space in approximately 2,000 Walmart stores across the United States. Vahdam's rise is a case study in how Indian food brands can capture global markets. The company sources teas, spices, and superfoods directly from Indian farms and estates, cutting out intermediaries and shipping fresh product to consumers. Revenue from operations reached 225.2 crore rupees (approximately $27 million) in the last reported fiscal year, with around 50 percent coming from the US market alone. "Foreign brands move to poor-quality teas from other tea-growing regions to compete on price points and earn higher margins," Sarda told YourStory. "Most of our teas are exported out in single-digit margins, with zero value addition, to be re-branded and sold at much higher margins." A fresh ₹25 crore investment from SIDBI Ventures is fuelling the next phase of expansion, with plans to strengthen the supply chain and deepen retail penetration in the US, Canada, Europe, and the UK. The company expects to turn operationally profitable this fiscal year. ## Beyond the Teabag Vahdam is not alone. The US market, valued at roughly $13 billion and historically dominated by iced tea and ready-to-drink formats, is showing signs of appetite for more sophisticated tea offerings. India's strength lies in varieties that American consumers are only beginning to discover — first-flush Darjeeling, Assam malty black teas, Nilgiri greens, and the vast world of flavoured chai blends built on cardamom, ginger, cinnamon, and clove. The chai category itself has evolved from a niche ethnic beverage to a mainstream American staple. Starbucks' chai latte, Trader Joe's spiced chai concentrate, and David's Tea's chai blends have normalised the flavour profile for millions of consumers who may never have tasted the real thing. What Indian brands bring to the table is authenticity — and increasingly, the story behind it.
Vahdam's Growth Story
›Founded in 2015 by Bala Sarda at age 23.
›Revenue reached ₹225.2 crore (~$27 million).
›50% of revenue comes from the US market.
›Plans to expand into Canada, Europe, and the UK.
Vahdam's collaboration with celebrity chef Vikas Khanna to launch 25 single-origin spices tailored for the US market signals a broader play. This is not just about tea anymore; it is about building an Indian wellness and flavour platform that competes globally. ## The Diaspora Bridge For the four-million-strong Indian American community, the expansion of Indian tea brands into mainstream retail hits a personal note. The morning chai that anchors so many NRI households — brewed strong with milk and sugar, the cardamom cracked fresh, the routine inherited from parents and grandparents — has always been difficult to replicate with the generic options available at American supermarkets. The appearance of brands like Vahdam, Organic India, and Tea India on Walmart and Amazon shelves means that the gap between the chai of memory and the chai of convenience is narrowing. When your Darjeeling comes shipped directly from an estate in West Bengal rather than through a European repackaging chain, the cup tastes different — and the story behind it matters. ## What Comes Next India faces structural challenges in tea exports. Weather volatility driven by climate change is making harvests less predictable. Labour costs at tea estates are rising. And the American market remains heavily oriented toward iced tea and ready-to-drink formats, categories where Argentine and Kenyan producers are strong.
The Chai Revolution
›Chai has evolved into a mainstream American beverage.
›Starbucks and Trader Joe's popularize chai flavors.
›Authenticity and direct sourcing enhance consumer appeal.
›Indian brands are bridging cultural gaps in tea offerings.
But the zero-duty advantage, combined with a growing premium segment and brands willing to invest in direct-to-consumer and retail channels, creates a window of opportunity that Indian exporters have not had in years. The Indian Tea Exporters Association sees potential to push US-bound volumes back to 18 to 20 million kilograms annually — and with brands building consumer loyalty rather than selling commodity bulk, the value per kilogram should rise significantly. The chai your nani brewed every morning is no longer just a family ritual. It is becoming a global product — and for once, the Indian producers who grow it are positioning themselves to capture the value.
